analysis.one_liner: Opens federal waters and the Arctic refuge to oil and gas drilling and blocks federal climate rules.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to four House committees and six subcommittees, none of which ever acted on it, and it died when the 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have rewritten a large swath of federal energy and environmental law in one stroke. It would have required the Interior Department to hold offshore oil and gas lease sales wherever companies wanted them, let drillers into the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge, approve TransCanada's Keystone XL pipeline by statute, and block any federal rule cutting carbon pollution until China, India, and Russia adopted matching rules. It would also have shortened environmental review, funneled almost all lawsuits over energy projects to a single Washington court with tight deadlines, and stopped reimbursing environmental groups' legal fees.
analysis.who_benefits: Oil and gas companies gain the most: mandated lease sales across the outer continental shelf, a competitive leasing program for the Arctic refuge's Coastal Plain with a 12.5% royalty, drilling permits decided within 20 days, and Keystone XL approved without a presidential permit. TransCanada gets its pipeline approved by law. Coal and other greenhouse-gas-emitting energy producers get existing and future EPA carbon rules nullified until China, India, and Russia adopt similar limits. Central Valley agricultural water users in California would keep receiving historical-maximum water deliveries even over endangered-species protections. Coastal states would receive shares of offshore drilling revenues starting in 2024, the Kaktovik Inupiat Corporation and Arctic Slope Regional Corporation receive land conveyances, and Drakes Bay Oyster Company gets its federal permits reinstated for at least a decade.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Oil and gas companies and TransCanada

how_it_helps.text: Requires the Interior Department to hold an offshore oil and gas lease sale within 180 days of enactment, and every 270 days after, in every outer continental shelf planning area where a commercial buyer exists, and lets petitioners force lease sales.

Repeals the legal ban on oil and gas leasing in the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge's Coastal Plain and directs the Bureau of Land Management to run a competitive leasing program there, with lease sales beginning within 22 months.
Requires the Interior Department to approve or reject an offshore drilling permit within 20 days, with only a 10-day window to resubmit a rejected application.

Declares that no presidential permit is needed for TransCanada's Keystone XL pipeline, deems its 2011 environmental impact statement final, approves the Nebraska route, and exempts the route from critical habitat designations.

Bars the EPA and any federal agency from enforcing any carbon dioxide or greenhouse gas reduction rule until the government certifies in writing that China, India, and Russia have adopted substantially similar reductions, and strips existing rules of force in the meantime.
Shares offshore drilling revenues with coastal states beginning in fiscal year 2024, and directs 90% of Coastal Plain lease revenues to the Treasury.
Requires Coastal Plain leases to include negotiated labor agreements for construction and production work and directs the government to encourage use of U.S. workers and U.S.-made equipment.

analysis.who_pays: If it had passed, the public would have paid in several currencies. Environmental review would have been cut short: a 1987 legislative impact statement would be deemed to satisfy the National Environmental Policy Act for Arctic refuge leasing, public comment on the refuge environmental study would be limited to 20 days, and the government would not have to analyze alternatives. Almost all lawsuits over federal energy projects would be funneled to the D.C. federal district court, with a 60-day filing deadline and automatic dismissal if not resolved in 180 days, and environmental groups could be barred from federal reimbursement of legal fees. Endangered species protections could not consider climate change, the President could no longer designate national monuments without Congress, and federal climate rules would be nullified until other countries acted. The oil under public lands and waters would be developed with most revenue going to companies, though leases carry a 12.5% royalty and 90% of refuge lease revenues would go to the Treasury.
analysis.who_pays_short: The public, through weakened environmental review

drawbacks.text: Deems decades-old environmental documents final: the April 1987 Coastal Plain impact statement would satisfy the National Environmental Policy Act for Arctic refuge pre-lease actions, and the August 2011 State Department statement would satisfy all requirements for Keystone XL, skipping current review.

Gives the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia exclusive jurisdiction over claims arising from federal energy leasing, requires filing within 60 days, and dismisses with prejudice any case not decided within 180 days, sharply narrowing the public's ability to challenge projects.

Prohibits federal payment of legal fees to environmental organizations in actions that reduce access to energy, minerals, water, grazing, or timber on federal land, making it harder for citizen groups to afford litigation.

Prohibits considering the impact of greenhouse gases or climate change on any species for any purpose under the Endangered Species Act, and strips existing EPA greenhouse gas rules of force until China, India, and Russia adopt similar reductions.
Amends the Antiquities Act so a president could no longer declare a national monument on federal land without an Act of Congress, ending a century-old protection mechanism.

Overturns the Interior Department's decision on Drakes Bay Oyster Company and bars converting Drakes Estero to wilderness, legislating the outcome of a specific contested permit rather than leaving it to existing law.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's benefits flow overwhelmingly to oil and gas producers: faster permits, mandated lease sales, refuge access, and a legislatively approved pipeline, plus revenue shares for coastal states and land for two Alaska Native corporations. Its costs fall broadly on the public: shortened environmental review, sharply limited court access, blocked climate regulation, and weakened species and monument protections. A supporter could fairly note the bill contained real protections, including a no-significant-adverse-effect standard for the refuge, 12.5% royalties, reclamation liability, caribou calving safeguards, and labor agreements; but the same bill deemed 30-year-old environmental documents final and made climate rules hostage to foreign governments' actions. As written, the trade ran mostly one way.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to four House committees and six subcommittees in its first weeks, none of which ever held a hearing or vote on it, and it expired when the 113th Congress ended in January 2015.

narrative.text: Rep. Rob Bishop of Utah introduced the bill on May 8, 2013, and it was referred to the House Committees on Natural Resources, Energy and Commerce, Transportation and Infrastructure, and Judiciary.

Between May 9 and June 14, 2013, it was referred to six subcommittees, covering railroads and pipelines, energy and power, energy and mineral resources, water and power, public lands, and regulatory reform.
No hearing, markup, or floor vote on the bill appears in the action history; the last recorded action was the June 14, 2013 subcommittee referral, and the Congress ended January 3, 2015.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died without a vote, no offshore lease sale mandates, no Arctic refuge leasing program, no Keystone approval by statute, and no nullification of federal climate rules took effect. Oil and gas companies gained nothing from this particular bill, while the public kept the existing environmental review processes, court access, and climate rules intact. Coastal states also did not receive the revenue shares the bill would have created.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: People who wanted the drilling and climate rules untouched

for.name: Rep. Rob Bishop
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on May 8, 2013 and chaired its progress only as far as committee referrals.

against.name: Chairs of the four House committees of referral
against.role: House Natural Resources, Energy and Commerce, Transportation and Infrastructure, and Judiciary committees
against.what_they_did: Took no recorded action after referral: no hearing, no markup, and no vote was ever scheduled in any of the four committees.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken, so no roll call exists; the bill had one Republican sponsor and zero cosponsors from either party.

industries.note: The bill mandates lease sales across the outer continental shelf wherever commercial buyers exist, opens the Arctic refuge to leasing, requires drilling permit decisions within 20 days, and deems old environmental studies final. Companies gain access to public resources on shortened review while the public absorbs the shortened scrutiny and the climate consequences of barred carbon rules.

The bill approves TransCanada's pipeline by statute, waives the presidential permit, and limits judicial review to direct appeal in the D.C. Circuit, removing the ordinary avenues that had kept the project tied up.

industries.industry: Coal and other greenhouse-gas-emitting energy producers
industries.note: Existing and future federal carbon rules would be nullified until the government certifies that China, India, and Russia adopted substantially similar reductions, a condition the bill's own findings acknowledge those countries had not met.

The bill bars federal reimbursement of these groups' legal fees in actions restricting energy, mineral, water, grazing, or timber access on federal land, and channels most energy project challenges to one court with 60-day and 180-day deadlines. These groups are the main vehicle citizens use to enforce environmental laws, so the limits fall on the public's ability to sue.
Federal and California water projects could not cut deliveries below the historical maximum under an endangered-species biological opinion, keeping more water flowing to farms in drought years.

industries.industry: Kaktovik Inupiat Corporation and Arctic Slope Regional Corporation
industries.note: The bill directs conveyance of surface and subsurface land estates to these Alaska Native corporations to settle long-standing entitlements under the Alaska Native Claims Settlement Act.

The bill reinstates this single company's federal operating permits at Point Reyes for at least 10 years and blocks wilderness designation of Drakes Estero. A working oyster farm stays in business, but Congress overrides an Interior Department decision and forecloses wilderness protection for a public estuary.
